You write one blog article for an online shop from a plan. You see the shop, the topic, the shop's products with the checked facts we hold about each (F1, F2…), the pages that may be linked, and the plan.

How to write it:
- In English, in the shop's tone, for the shop's audience. 700–2000 words. Open with a short paragraph that answers the search directly, then the sections as "##" headings ("###" below them if needed). No "#" heading: the title is set separately. Use a list or a table where it genuinely helps the reader.
- You may speak as the shop ("in our range", "we stock"). Never claim experience: no testing, trying, favourites, "in our experience", what customers say, and no "I".
- Never mention a price, a discount, delivery, competitors or other shops. Respect the never-say list.

Every product claim cites its facts. After any sentence that says something about one of our products, put the facts it rests on in square brackets just before the full stop: "It is dishwasher safe [F5]." or "[F2, F7]". The sentence may say only what those facts say. Every sentence that names one of our products needs a citation.

Numbers. A number about our products must appear in a fact the sentence cites. A number that is general knowledge, not about our products (a common ratio, temperature or time), is allowed only if it is well established and uncontroversial; mark its sentence with [G] before the full stop, and do not name any of our products in that sentence. Never invent statistics, studies or survey figures. Headings carry no brackets, so keep numbers out of headings unless they count the article's own items.

Links and products. Link only to the pages and products you were given, by their reference as the address: [our ceramic dripper](P1), [our brewing guide](L2). Never write a web address. To show a product card, put {{P1}} alone on its own line where the card should appear; show each card once.

Before you answer, read every sentence once more. A sentence with a digit in it carries [F…] for a fact that contains that number, or [G]. A sentence that names one of our products, even just to recommend it, carries [F…]. Fix any that do not.

Also give: meta_description, 70–170 characters, plain, no brackets; slug, lowercase words joined by hyphens.

{"title":"How to Reuse Candle Jars: Cleaning Tips and Second-Life Ideas","meta_description":"Learn how to get leftover wax out of a finished candle jar, clean it and remove the label, then turn it into a planter, storage jar or pen cup.","slug":"how-to-reuse-candle-jars","markdown":"To reuse a candle jar, stop burning while a thin layer of wax is still in the bottom and let the jar cool completely. Then pop the leftover wax out by freezing it or melting it with hot water, scrape off the wick tab, and wash the jar in warm soapy water. Peel off the label and your jar is ready to be a planter, a pen cup, a spice jar or even a brand-new candle. Here's how to do each step without cracking the glass or making a mess.

## When a Candle Is Really Done

A candle is finished a little before the wax runs out. Most candle makers suggest stopping a burn when about half an inch of wax is left in the bottom [G]. That last layer protects the base of the container from the flame.

If you keep burning right down to the bottom, the flame and the hot wick tab can sit almost directly on the base of the jar. That can overheat the container, scorch the surface underneath, and in the worst case crack the glass. So when you see the wax getting shallow, blow it out and call it a day.

Before you start any cleanup, let the jar cool all the way down. Warm glass or ceramic plus cold water or a cold freezer is a recipe for cracks. Give it a few hours on the counter, or leave it overnight to be safe.

## Getting the Leftover Wax Out

There are three easy ways to get that last bit of wax out. Pick the one that suits your jar and how patient you're feeling.

### The freezer method

Pop the cooled jar into the freezer for a few hours or overnight. Wax shrinks as it gets cold, so it pulls away from the sides of the container. Run a butter knife around the edge and the wax will often come out in one satisfying disc. If it's stubborn, tap the jar gently upside down over a towel.

This method is best for jars with straight sides or a wide opening. A narrow neck can trap the wax disc inside.

### The hot-water method

Set the jar in the sink and fill it with hot water from the kettle, leaving a little space at the top. The heat melts the wax, which floats up to the surface. Let the water cool completely, and the wax will harden into a layer you can lift right off.

One caution: never pour very hot water into a jar that has just come out of the freezer. Sudden temperature changes are what crack glass, so let the jar sit at room temperature first.

### Warming and pouring off

You can also stand the jar in a saucepan of gently simmering water, like a mini double boiler. Once the wax has melted, carefully pour it into an old tin or a container lined with paper, then wipe the inside of the jar with a paper towel while it's still warm. Don't pour melted wax down the sink, as it hardens in the pipes.

### Soy and coconut-soy waxes are easy to clean up

The kind of wax in your candle makes a real difference here. Our [Sea Salt Soy Candle](P1) is made of 100% soy wax [F2]. Our [Cedar Wood-Wick Candle](P2) uses a coconut and soy wax blend [F13]. Soy and coconut-soy waxes are soft, natural waxes that tend to release from a container without much fuss, and any thin film left behind usually washes away with warm soapy water. Harder waxes, by contrast, can need more scraping.

### Removing the wick tab

At the bottom of most container candles is a small metal disc that holds the wick in place. Once the wax is out, slide a butter knife or a spoon under the tab and pop it up. If it's glued down, a little hot water around it will usually soften the adhesive enough to lift it.

## Cleaning and Removing Labels

With the wax gone, it's time to make the jar look new again.

- **Wash it well.** Use warm water, dish soap and a soft sponge to clear off any waxy film and soot. A bottle brush helps with corners and narrow openings.
- **Peel the label.** Soak the jar in warm soapy water for a while and most paper labels will slide off.
- **Tackle sticky residue.** Rub a little cooking oil onto any leftover glue, let it sit, then wipe it away. A paste of baking soda and oil works well as a gentle scrub for stubborn spots.
- **Dry thoroughly.** Let the jar air-dry completely, inside and out, before you fill it, especially if you plan to store dry goods like tea or spices.

### Glass versus ceramic

Glass is easy to clean, but it can scratch, so skip metal scouring pads and stick to soft sponges and baking soda. Hold glass up to the light once it's dry to check for any cloudy film you missed.

Ceramic needs a slightly different touch. Glazed surfaces wipe clean easily, but an unglazed base or rim can soak up oil and soapy water, so go easy on the oil method around those areas and give the vessel extra drying time. Avoid abrasive scrubbers on glazes and any printed or painted finishes, since they can dull the surface.

## Ideas for Your Empty Jar

Once your jar is clean and dry, the fun part begins. Here are some favourite second lives for an empty candle container:

- **Bathroom storage:** cotton swabs, cotton pads, hair ties or bath salts.
- **Desk organizer:** a pen and pencil cup, or a home for paper clips and sticky notes.
- **Makeup brush holder:** wide, heavy jars keep brushes upright and tidy.
- **Small planter:** succulents and cacti are perfect for jars without drainage holes. Add a layer of pebbles at the bottom so roots don't sit in water, and water sparingly.
- **Pantry jar:** loose-leaf tea, spices, coffee beans or small snacks, ideally in a jar with a lid.
- **Mini vase:** a few garden stems, dried flowers or a single bloom on a bedside table.
- **A brand-new candle:** buy candle wax and a pre-tabbed wick, stick the wick to the bottom, melt the wax in a double boiler and pour. It's a lovely weekend project.

## Tidewell Jars Worth Keeping

Some candle containers are simply nicer to hold onto than others, and we choose our vessels with a second life in mind.

{{P1}}

The [Sea Salt Soy Candle](P1) comes in an 8 oz amber glass jar [F1, F7]. Its jar has a tin lid [F8]. A lidded jar is one of the most useful things to have around the house, because it keeps contents covered and dust-free. Think loose tea, bath salts, cotton pads or a stash of hair ties. Amber glass also looks great lined up on a bathroom shelf or open pantry.

{{P2}}

The [Cedar Wood-Wick Candle](P2) comes in a 12 oz ceramic vessel [F11, F16]. That vessel is reusable, so it's made to stay on your shelf long after the candle is gone [F17]. A sturdy ceramic container makes a handsome planter for a small succulent, a steady desk cup for pens and scissors, or a holder for makeup brushes. Just follow the ceramic cleaning tips above and give it plenty of time to dry.

## Enjoying the Candle Before the Jar

Of course, the best part of a candle comes before the jar is empty. A few simple habits help you get every hour out of it.

The Sea Salt Soy Candle has a burn time of about 45 hours [F6]. It has a cotton wick that is lead-free [F4, F5]. Its scent notes are sea salt, driftwood and sage [F9]. Each one is poured by hand in Portland, Maine [F3].

The Cedar Wood-Wick Candle has a burn time of about 60 hours [F15]. Its cherry-wood wick crackles as it burns [F14]. For the best flame, trim that wood wick to 3 mm before each burn [F18]. Its scent notes are cedar, black pepper and vetiver [F19].

Whichever candle you choose, burn it with care, stop while there's still a thin layer of wax left, and you'll end up with a clean, useful jar to enjoy for years. Ready for your next one? Browse our full range of [candles](L1)."}
